intro: A league is more than a set of teams. It is a private association with founding papers, members who vote, officers who enforce rules and courts that can review them. In 1744 an Edinburgh golf club wrote thirteen articles for one competition. In 1917 hockey owners in Montreal formed a whole new league to leave out one owner. In 2014 basketball's owners moved to take a team away from one of their own.

This unit follows two kinds of governing bodies. The first chapter looks at clubs, leagues and commissioners: vote thresholds, lifetime bans, gambling rules and the idea of amateurism, which split English cricket into Gentlemen and Players until 1962. The second chapter comes home to the public high school. It looks at who took charge of school teams, the civic rituals of a game night, open-meeting and public-record laws, booster clubs, budgets and the question of whether a game makes money.

By the end, you can explain who wrote a rule and who was left out of the room. You can name the Illinois laws that keep school money open to the public. You can build an argument about whether a school district should publish what a game earns and costs, using dates, documents and court cases.
bigQuestion: Who holds power in a league or a school sports program, and how can the people outside the room hold that power to account?

timeline.t: The Gentlemen Golfers of Leith write thirteen articles, the oldest known golf rules
The Marylebone Cricket Club is founded in London and soon issues revised Laws of Cricket
The Public Schools Athletic League is founded in New York City
Hockey owners form the National Hockey League in Montreal without Eddie Livingstone
Arena owners found the Basketball Association of America in New York
Illinois passes its Open Meetings Act
English cricket ends the divide between Gentlemen and Players
Pete Rose accepts permanent ineligibility from baseball
Rugby union's world body declares the sport open to paid players
Santa Fe v. Doe strikes down a school-sponsored pregame prayer
The University of Illinois retires the Chief Illiniwek halftime performance
The NBA bans Clippers owner Donald Sterling for life

words.d: the body trusted to keep a set of rules and decide how they change
an organization's founding document, naming its members, how they vote and how members can be removed
a club's right, granted by its league, to play in a certain place
a larger share of votes than a simple majority, such as three-fourths
a league official, hired by the owners, with power over the whole sport
the belief that sport is best played for its own sake, without pay
a set of beliefs that seems natural to its holders but can serve some groups more than others
a person or group whose actions count as government action under the Constitution
a repeated public ceremony that expresses belonging to a town or nation
a document a public body creates or keeps about its business
a draft budget shown to the public before a board adopts the final one
a group, usually of parents and fans, that raises money for a school team

test.q: Which body became the keeper of the Laws of Cricket?
test.why: The MCC, founded in 1787, issued revised laws in 1788 and became their custodian.

test.q: Why did hockey owners form a new league in 1917?
choices: to leave out an owner their old constitution protected
test.why: The owners formed the NHL so that Eddie Livingstone would not be a member.

test.q: Why do many historians call amateurism an ideology?
choices: It was written by players' unions
It seemed natural but served some groups more than others
It was part of the U.S. Constitution
test.why: Amateur rules, like cricket's split into Gentlemen and Players, often favored those who could afford to play unpaid.

test.q: What vote would NBA owners have needed to end Donald Sterling's ownership?
test.why: The NBA constitution lets the Board of Governors end an owner's membership by a three-fourths vote.
Owners create and fill the commissioner's office and give it power over the sport.

test.q: What did Commissioner Manfred rule about permanent ineligibility in 2025?
test.why: Manfred ruled the ban ends at death and removed Pete Rose and others from the list.

test.q: What happened to rugby union in August 1995?
choices: It joined the Olympics for the first time
Its world body declared it open to paid players
It adopted the Laws of Cricket
test.why: The International Rugby Football Board declared rugby union an open game on August 26, 1995.

test.q: What did Brentwood Academy (2001) decide about a state athletic association?
choices: It can be a state actor
test.why: The Court ruled 5 to 4 that the Tennessee association's actions counted as government action.

test.q: What does the Illinois Open Meetings Act require of a school board?
choices: posting an agenda at least 48 hours before a regular meeting
letting boosters vote on the budget
test.why: The 1957 act requires open votes and an agenda posted at least 48 hours ahead.

test.q: Which law lets anyone request a district's stadium invoices?
choices: the Illinois Freedom of Information Act
test.why: The Illinois FOIA of 1984, rewritten in 2010, presumes public records are open.

test.q: What did the Court decide in Santa Fe v. Doe (2000)?
choices: A coach's private prayer is protected
A school-sponsored pregame prayer over the loudspeaker was not allowed
test.why: The Court ruled 6 to 3 that the pregame prayer violated the Establishment Clause.

test.q: How can booster gifts raise a Title IX issue?
choices: Boosters must register with the IOC
Booster money must go to the state
Benefits athletes receive count, whatever their source
test.why: The Office for Civil Rights looks at the benefits athletes actually receive.

test.q: Why is one game's profit hard to state as a single number?
choices: Its costs sit in different funds, so it depends on which costs are counted
Districts are not allowed to count money
Only the IHSA keeps the records
Ticket sales are secret by law
test.why: Lights, buses, police and gate money may sit in separate budget funds.

test.q: When can the public read an Illinois district's draft budget?
choices: for at least thirty days before the board adopts it
test.why: The tentative budget must be open to inspection for at least thirty days, followed by a public hearing.

test.q: Which two bodies are alike because a private group's rules came to govern many others?
choices: the MCC and the St Andrews golf club
the Sherman Act and Title IX
test.why: Other clubs chose to follow the MCC's cricket laws and the St Andrews club's golf rulings.

write.prompt: Should an Illinois school district publish the profit or loss of its Friday-night games? Argue your answer. Cite at least three of the unit's dates or documents, such as the Open Meetings Act, the Illinois FOIA, the thirty-day budget display, Title IX or Brentwood Academy (2001).
tips: Name each law, case or document you cite, with its year.
Say which costs you would count and why.
Answer the strongest point on the other side, such as the value of a civic ritual.
Use unit terms such as public record, booster club and state actor.
Keep facts separate from your opinion, and show how each fact supports it.
